lesson.title: The Proton: The Particle That Names the Element
lesson.summary: Protons are the positively charged nuclear particles whose count defines which element an atom is, from hydrogen to uranium and beyond.
lesson.body:
Every atom is built from three subatomic particles: protons, neutrons, and electrons. Of the three, the proton carries the most fundamental job, because it decides which element you are looking at. A proton is a positively charged particle with a mass of about 1.673 times 10 to the negative 27 kilograms, roughly 1.007 atomic mass units, and a charge of positive one elementary unit, equal to about 1.602 times 10 to the negative 19 coulombs. It lives packed tightly inside the atomic nucleus alongside neutrons, held there by the strong nuclear force, a short range force powerful enough to overcome the electrical repulsion between positively charged protons crammed into a space smaller than a trillionth of a meter across.

Why does proton count matter so much? Because chemical identity is not about mass or size, it is about proton number. Add or remove a neutron and you get a different isotope of the same element. Add or remove an electron and you get an ion, still the same element. But change the number of protons, and the atom becomes an entirely different element with entirely different chemistry. This is why proton count, called the atomic number, sits at the top of every box on the periodic table. It is the one number that never changes without changing what the atom fundamentally is, and it is the concept that proton count builds toward directly.

Consider carbon. Every carbon atom, whether in diamond, in your body, or in carbon dioxide, has exactly six protons. Take away one proton and those six become five, and the atom is now boron, a completely different element with different bonding behavior and different physical properties. Add one proton instead and you get seven, nitrogen, the gas that makes up about 78 percent of the air you breathe. No ordinary chemical reaction can change proton number. Burning, dissolving, and reacting can turn carbon into carbon dioxide, but never into nitrogen. Only nuclear processes, occurring in stars, nuclear reactors, or radioactive decay, can change how many protons a nucleus holds.

A useful worked example makes the distinction concrete. An aluminum ion written as Al3+ has lost three electrons compared to a neutral aluminum atom, but it still has 13 protons, because it is still aluminum, just positively charged. Ionization changes electron count, never proton count. Likewise, the common stable isotope aluminum-27 and the rarer aluminum-26 differ only in neutron count, both carrying 13 protons in the nucleus. Protons were first identified experimentally by Ernest Rutherford in the early twentieth century, when he observed that bombarding nitrogen gas with alpha particles knocked positively charged particles free from the nucleus, particles that turned out to be identical no matter which element they came from.

This distinction, protons fixing identity while electrons and neutrons vary independently, is the foundation for nearly everything that follows in atomic structure. Understanding that the proton count alone defines the element is what makes concepts like atomic number, isotopes, and ion formation possible to reason about clearly, since each of those ideas depends on knowing exactly which particle count is fixed and which ones are free to change.
